title: SQL Joins
interviewAnswer: INNER JOIN returns matching rows; LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left side and fills unmatched right-side columns with NULL; FULL OUTER JOIN keeps rows from both sides. Choose based on what records must survive the join.
why: Joins test whether you understand relational grain, keys and duplicate amplification—not just SQL syntax. They are central to feature building, analytics and ETL.
intuition: A join decides which rows survive when two tables are connected by a key. Before writing SQL, state the grain of each table and whether the key is one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many.
deepDive: INNER JOIN keeps only matching rows. LEFT JOIN preserves every left-side row and fills unmatched right columns with NULL. FULL OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched rows from both sides. A many-to-many join multiplies rows, which is often the source of silent metric inflation. Join predicates belong in ON when they define matching logic; filters in WHERE can accidentally turn a LEFT JOIN into INNER-like behavior by removing NULL matches.
workedExample: customers has one row per customer while orders has many rows per customer. Joining them creates one row per order, not one row per customer. If you later average a customer-level feature without re-aggregating, heavy buyers are overrepresented.
code:
SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
commonMistakes: Ignoring table grain and creating duplicate amplification.
Filtering right-table columns in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN and unintentionally dropping unmatched rows.
Joining on non-unique or dirty keys without checking cardinality.
followUps: What happens in a many-to-many join?
How do NULLs behave in joins?
How would you detect duplicate amplification?
production: In feature pipelines, validate join cardinality, row counts and uniqueness before/after joins. Point-in-time joins are essential to prevent temporal leakage.
